claim: Using single-cell RNA-sequencing, five distinct NK cell clusters were identified in murine bone marrow based on transcriptome.
source: Based on transcriptome, we identified five distinct NK cell clusters and define their relative developmental maturity in the bone marrow.
evidence: The manuscript describes the identification of five NK clusters through scRNA-seq analysis and presents this in Figure 1C.

claim: Half of the mTORC2-deficient NK cells belong to the least mature NK cluster.
source: Transcriptome-based machine-learning classifiers revealed that half of the mTORC2-deficient NK cells belongs to the least mature NK cluster.
evidence: Machine-learning classification results shown in Figure 4E demonstrate approximately 50% of Rictor-deficient NK cells classified as iNK cluster.

claim: Loss of mTORC2 results in increased expression of signature genes representing immature NK cells.
source: Mechanistically, loss of mTORC2 results in an increased expression of signature genes representing immature NK cells.
evidence: Module score analysis in Figure 3E shows elevated expression of iNK signature genes in Rictor-deficient NK cells.

claim: mTORC2 regulates the expression of T-bet through AktS473-FoxO1 axis.
source: Since mTORC2 regulates the expression of T-bet through AktS473-FoxO1 axis, we further characterized the T-bet-deficient NK cells and found an augmented immature transcriptomic signature.
evidence: This is based on previous work by the authors (Yang et al., 2018) and is validated by rescue experiments shown in Figure 7.

claim: T-bet-deficient NK cells have an augmented immature transcriptomic signature.
source: Since mTORC2 regulates the expression of T-bet through AktS473-FoxO1 axis, we further characterized the T-bet-deficient NK cells and found an augmented immature transcriptomic signature.
evidence: Figure 5E and 5F demonstrate up-regulation of immature NK signature genes in T-bet-deficient NK cells.

claim: Deletion of Foxo1 restores the expression of T-bet in Rictor-deficient NK cells.
source: Moreover, deletion of Foxo1 restores the expression of T-bet and corrects the abnormal expression of immature NK genes.
evidence: Figure 7—figure supplement 1E shows rescued T-bet expression in Rictor/Foxo1 double knockout NK cells.

claim: Deletion of Foxo1 corrects the abnormal expression of immature NK genes in Rictor-deficient NK cells.
source: Moreover, deletion of Foxo1 restores the expression of T-bet and corrects the abnormal expression of immature NK genes.
evidence: Figure 7D and 7E demonstrate reduced expression of iNK signature genes in Rictor/Foxo1 double knockout compared to Rictor single knockout.

claim: The mTORC2-AktS473-FoxO1-T-bet axis suppresses the transcriptional signature of immature NK cells.
source: Collectively, our study reveals a novel role for mTORC2-AktS473-FoxO1-T-bet axis in suppressing the transcriptional signature of immature NK cells.
evidence: This is supported by the combined data from Rictor, T-bet, and Foxo1 knockout experiments showing increased immature gene expression and rescue upon Foxo1 deletion.

claim: The expression of IL-15/IL-2 receptor β chain (CD122) is the hallmark of commitment to the NK cell lineage from the common lymphoid progenitor (CLP) cells in mouse bone marrow.
source: In the bone marrow (BM) of mice, the expression of IL-15/IL-2 receptor β chain (CD122) is the hallmark of commitment to the NK cell lineage from the common lymphoid progenitor (CLP) cells (Rosmaraki et al., 2001).
evidence: This claim is supported by citation to Rosmaraki et al., 2001.

claim: The canonical definition of NK progenitor (NKP) is a Lin−CD122+ cell without cell surface expression of NK-lineage marker NK1.1.
source: Thus, the canonical definition of NK progenitor (NKP) is a Lin−CD122+ cell without cell surface expression of NK-lineage marker NK1.1.
evidence: This is established knowledge in the field based on the previous statement about CD122 expression.

claim: Approximately only one in ten Lin−CD122+NK1.1− cells can give rise to NK cells in vitro.
source: However, the Lin−CD122+NK1.1− cells are still a heterogeneous population as approximately only one in ten cells can give rise to NK cells in vitro (Vosshenrich and Di Santo, 2013).
evidence: This claim is supported by citation to Vosshenrich and Di Santo, 2013.

claim: Lin−Flt3−CD27+2B4+CD127+CD122+NK1.1− cells have a 50% chance to develop into NK cells in vitro.
source: Recently, the definition of NKPs has been refined to Lin−Flt3−CD27+2B4+CD127+CD122+NK1.1− cells which have a 50% chance to develop into NK cells in vitro (Carotta et al., 2011; Fathman et al., 2011).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to Carotta et al., 2011 and Fathman et al., 2011.

claim: The Lin−CD122+NK1.1+CD27+CD49b− population represents the least mature NK cells.
source: The Lin−CD122+NK1.1+CD27+CD49b− population represents the least mature NK cells (Di Santo, 2006; Kim et al., 2002; Williams et al., 2000; Arase et al., 2001).
evidence: This claim is supported by multiple citations: Di Santo, 2006; Kim et al., 2002; Williams et al., 2000; Arase et al., 2001.

claim: Murine NK cells are classified into three developmental stages based on CD27 and CD11b expression: CD27+CD11b− (CD27 single positive), CD27+CD11b+ (double positive), and CD27−CD11b+ (CD11b single positive).
source: Subsequent to the expression of CD49b, the developmental stages of murine NK cells further classified into three stages based on two cell surface markers CD27 and CD11b (Kim et al., 2002; Hayakawa and Smyth, 2006). The relatively immature CD27+CD11b− (CD27 single positive, SP) NK cells develop into CD27−CD11b+ (CD11b single positive, SP) terminally mature with a transitional stage of CD27+CD11b+ (double positive, DP) cells (Chiossone et al., 2009).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to Kim et al., 2002; Hayakawa and Smyth, 2006; and Chiossone et al., 2009.

claim: Terminal CD11b SP NK cells are marked with expression of KLRG1.
source: The terminal CD11b SP NK cells are also marked with expression of KLRG1 (Huntington et al., 2007).
evidence: This claim is supported by citation to Huntington et al., 2007.

claim: Ets-1 and PU.1 regulate the transition from CLPs to NKPs.
source: Ets-1 and PU.1 regulate the transition from CLPs to NKPs, while E4BP4 is critical in the induction of CD122 and NKP commitment (Barton et al., 1998; Colucci et al., 2001; Gascoyne et al., 2009; Kamizono et al., 2009).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to Barton et al., 1998 and Colucci et al., 2001.

claim: E4BP4 is critical in the induction of CD122 and NKP commitment.
source: Ets-1 and PU.1 regulate the transition from CLPs to NKPs, while E4BP4 is critical in the induction of CD122 and NKP commitment (Barton et al., 1998; Colucci et al., 2001; Gascoyne et al., 2009; Kamizono et al., 2009).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to Gascoyne et al., 2009 and Kamizono et al., 2009.

claim: E4BP4 induces the expression of Id2 and Eomes, both of which are critical in immature NK cells development.
source: E4BP4 also induces the expression of Id2 and Eomes, both of which are critical in immature NK cells development and the transition to the later stages (Male et al., 2014; Yokota et al., 1999; Boos et al., 2007; Delconte et al., 2016; Gordon et al., 2012).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to Male et al., 2014; Yokota et al., 1999; Boos et al., 2007; Delconte et al., 2016; Gordon et al., 2012.

claim: T-bet and Zeb2 are critical for terminal NK cell maturation.
source: T-bet and Zeb2 have been shown to be critical for terminal NK cell maturation (Townsend et al., 2004; van Helden et al., 2015).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to Townsend et al., 2004 and van Helden et al., 2015.

claim: PDK1 is required for the induction of E4BP4 during early NK cell development.
source: PDK1 is required for the induction of E4BP4 during early NK cell development (Yang et al., 2015).
evidence: This claim is supported by citation to Yang et al., 2015.

claim: mTORC1 is required for the expression of Eomes and the transition from CD27 SP to DP NK stage.
source: We have previously reported that mTORC1 is required for the expression of Eomes and the transition from CD27 SP to DP NK stage, while mTORC2 is required for the terminal CD11b SP NK cell maturation through mTORC2-AktS473-FoxO1 axis (Yang et al., 2018).
evidence: This claim is supported by citation to Yang et al., 2018, which is the authors' previous work.

claim: mTORC2 is required for the terminal CD11b SP NK cell maturation through mTORC2-AktS473-FoxO1 axis.
source: We have previously reported that mTORC1 is required for the expression of Eomes and the transition from CD27 SP to DP NK stage, while mTORC2 is required for the terminal CD11b SP NK cell maturation through mTORC2-AktS473-FoxO1 axis (Yang et al., 2018).
evidence: This claim is supported by citation to Yang et al., 2018, which is the authors' previous work.

claim: NK cells deficient in Id2, Eomes or Gata3 all fail to progress from CD27 SP to DP stages.
source: Based on the CD27/CD11b-defined stages, NK cells deficient in Id2, Eomes or Gata3 all fail to progress from CD27 SP to DP stages (Delconte et al., 2016; Gordon et al., 2012; Ali et al., 2016).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to Delconte et al., 2016; Gordon et al., 2012; and Ali et al., 2016.

claim: Crinier et al., 2018 identified a novel population in the mouse spleen and revealed conserved NK subsets in human and mice using scRNA-seq.
source: Crinier et al., 2018 has explored the murine and human NK cells from spleen and blood using single-cell RNA-sequencing (scRNA-seq) technology and identified a novel population in the mouse spleen and revealed the conserved NK subsets in human and mice.
evidence: This claim is supported by citation to Crinier et al., 2018.

claim: CD3ε−CD122+ cells from bone marrow contain three major cell types: conventional NK cells, innate lymphoid cells 1 (ILC1), and cells with high transcripts contents of Cd3d/e/g.
source: The single-cell transcriptome analyses revealed three major cell types from the CD3ε−CD122+ compartment: conventional NK cells, innate lymphoid cells 1 (ILC1), and cells with high transcripts contents of Cd3d/e/g.
evidence: This is demonstrated in Figure 1A and 1B showing distinct clusters with different marker expression.

claim: Five distinct NK developmental subsets were identified: an immature NK (iNK) cell cluster, three transitional NK (transNK) cell clusters, and a terminally mature NK (termNK) cell cluster.
source: We define five distinct NK developmental subsets: an immature NK (iNK) cell cluster, three transitional NK (transNK) cell clusters, and a terminally mature NK (termNK) cell cluster.
evidence: This is shown in Figure 1C with five distinct clusters identified through unbiased clustering analysis.

claim: More than 65% of T-bet-deficient NK cells are classified into the least mature iNK cluster.
source: Strikingly, more than 65% of T-bet-deficient NK cells are classified into the least mature iNK cluster and the expression of immature NK signature genes are highly up-regulated in the T-bet-deficient NK cells.
evidence: This is demonstrated in Figure 5D showing machine-learning classification results.

claim: The expression of immature NK signature genes are highly up-regulated in T-bet-deficient NK cells.
source: Strikingly, more than 65% of T-bet-deficient NK cells are classified into the least mature iNK cluster and the expression of immature NK signature genes are highly up-regulated in the T-bet-deficient NK cells.
evidence: This is shown in Figure 5E and 5F with specific genes listed and their expression levels compared.

claim: Deletion of Foxo1 rescues the developmental impairment of Rictor-deficient NK cells defined by both cell surface markers and developmental transcriptome markers.
source: Finally, deletion of Foxo1 successfully rescued the developmental impairment of Rictor-deficient NK cells defined by both cell surface markers and developmental transcriptome markers.
evidence: This is demonstrated in Figure 7A, 7B, 7C, and 7D showing rescue of maturation phenotypes.

claim: Different housing conditions can result in alteration in the transcriptome profile that leads to individual-specific phenotype in scRNA-seq analysis of NK cells.
source: These data revealed that different housing conditions could result in alteration in the transcriptome profile that leads to individual-specific phenotype in scRNA-seq analysis of NK cells.
evidence: This is based on the observation in Figure 1—figure supplement 1D and E showing separate clustering of mice from different facilities.

claim: Cluster #1 represents conventional NK cells with high expression of Ncr1 and three subunits (Klrb1a, Klrb1b, and Klrb1c) of NK1.1.
source: Through exploring the differential expressed genes (DEGs) of each cluster, we found that Cluster #1 were conventional NK cells with high expression of Ncr1 and three subunits (Klrb1a, Klrb1b, and Klrb1c) of NK1.1 and comprised majority of the CD3ε−CD122+ cells (Figure 1A and B).
evidence: This is demonstrated in Figure 1B showing expression levels of these markers.

claim: Cluster #2 contains cycling cells indicated by the expression of Mki67.
source: The expression of Mki67 indicated that cells in Cluster #2 were cycling (Figure 1B).
evidence: This is shown in Figure 1B with Mki67 expression pattern.

claim: Cluster #3 contains ILC1 cells indicated by the high expression of Tmem176a/b and Cxcr6.
source: Cluster #3 contained ILC1 cells indicated by the high expression of Tmem176a/b and Cxcr6 (Figure 1B; Robinette et al., 2015).
evidence: This is shown in Figure 1B and supported by citation to Robinette et al., 2015.

claim: Ncr1 and Klrb1a/b/c are more abundantly expressed in the ILC1 cluster than in the NK cluster.
source: Notably, Ncr1 and Klrb1a/b/c were abundantly expressed in the ILC1 cluster that was higher than the NK cluster (Figure 1B).
evidence: This is demonstrated in Figure 1B showing comparative expression levels.

claim: Cluster #4 is marked with high expression of Cd3d/e/g and low Ncr1 and Klrb1a/b/c expression.
source: Cluster #4 was marked with high expression of Cd3d/e/g and low Ncr1 and Klrb1a/b/c expression (Figure 1B).
evidence: This is shown in Figure 1B with expression patterns of these markers.

claim: The Cd3high population has been reported in scRNA-seq dataset of group 1 ILC in the lung and is potentially related to NK-T lineage.
source: This population has been reported before in the scRNA-seq dataset of group 1 ILC in the lung and is potentially related to NK-T lineage (Ferrari de Andrade et al., 2018).
evidence: This claim is supported by citation to Ferrari de Andrade et al., 2018 and includes speculation about lineage relationship.

claim: Cells in Cluster #5 were activated by inflammatory stimuli as evidenced by high expression of interferon-induced genes.
source: Cells in Cluster #5 were activated by inflammatory stimuli as made evident by the high expression of interferon-induced genes (Figure 1B).
evidence: This is shown in Figure 1B and represents an inference about cell state based on gene expression.

claim: Cluster #1 represents the most immature NK cells with high expression of Cd27 and low expression of Itgam (CD11b) and Ly49s.
source: Based on the expression of several NK cell maturation-defining markers, we found that Cluster #1 represented the most immature NK cells with high expression of Cd27 and low expression of Itgam (CD11b) and Ly49s (Klra1/3/4/7/8/9) (Figure 1E and Figure 1—figure supplement 1F).
evidence: This is demonstrated in Figure 1E and Figure 1—figure supplement 1F showing expression patterns.

claim: The immature nature of Cluster #1 is supported by high transcriptional expression of Ltb, Thy1, Cd3d/g, and Cd7, all of which are highly expressed in immature CD27 SP NK cells.
source: The immature nature of Cluster #1 was further supported by the high transcriptional expression of Ltb, Thy1, Cd3d/g, and Cd7 (Figure 1F), all of which have been shown to be highly expressed in the immature CD27 SP NK cells (Chiossone et al., 2009).
evidence: This is shown in Figure 1F and supported by citation to Chiossone et al., 2009.

claim: Cluster #5 represents terminally mature NK cells marked by low expression of Cd27 and high expression of Itgam (CD11b) and Klrg1.
source: In comparison, the low expression of Cd27 and high expression of Itgam (CD11b) and Klrg1 marked Cluster #5 as the terminally mature NK cells (Figure 1E).
evidence: This is demonstrated in Figure 1E showing expression patterns of maturation markers.

claim: The high expression of functional molecules including Gzma and Gzmb demonstrates the terminal maturity of cells in Cluster #5.
source: The high expression of functional molecules including Gzma and Gzmb further demonstrated the terminal maturity of cells in Cluster #5 (Figure 1F).
evidence: This is shown in Figure 1F with expression of effector molecules.

claim: TransNK1 cluster has high expression of genes encoding proteins involved in ribosomal biogenesis including ribonucleoproteins (Nop10, Nhp2, Gar1, Npm1, Npm3), RNA modification enzymes (Mettl1, Ddx21, Fbl), and GTPase related to nucleocytoplasmic transport (Ran, Ranbp1).
source: TransNK1 represented a unique NK sub-population with high expression of genes encoding proteins involved in ribosomal biogenesis including ribonucleoproteins (Nop10, Nhp2, Gar1, Npm1, Npm3), RNA modification enzymes (Mettl1, Ddx21, Fbl), and GTPase related to nucleocytoplasmic transport (Ran, Ranbp1).
evidence: This is based on analysis of differentially expressed genes in the transNK1 cluster.

claim: TransNK1 cluster has high expression of genes encoding ribosomal subunits.
source: We also found high expression of genes encoding the ribosomal subunits in this cluster (Figure 1—figure supplement 2A).
evidence: This is shown in Figure 1—figure supplement 2A with module score analysis.

claim: Transcription factors MYC and E2F are significantly enriched in transNK1 cluster compared to all other cells.
source: Gene set enrichment analysis (GSEA) revealed significantly enrichment of transcription factors MYC and E2F in transNK1 cluster compared to all other cells, both of which are involved in cell growth and proliferation (Figure 1—figure supplement 2B; Conacci-Sorrell et al., 2014; Chen et al., 2009).
evidence: This is shown in Figure 1—figure supplement 2B and supported by citations to Conacci-Sorrell et al., 2014 and Chen et al., 2009.

claim: Major metabolic pathways including glycolysis, oxidative phosphorylation and fatty acid metabolism are enriched in transNK1 cluster.
source: We also found major metabolic pathways were enriched in this cluster including glycolysis, oxidative phosphorylation and fatty acid metabolism (Figure 1—figure supplement 2C).
evidence: This is shown in Figure 1—figure supplement 2C through GSEA analysis.

claim: TransNK2 cluster is featured with high expression of Ly49 family members especially Klra4 (Ly49D) and Klra8 (Ly49H).
source: This cluster was featured with high expression of Ly49 family members especially Klra4 (Ly49D) and Klra8 (Ly49H) (Figure 1F and Figure 1—figure supplement 1F).
evidence: This is demonstrated in Figure 1F and Figure 1—figure supplement 1F showing expression patterns.

claim: TransNK3 cluster has multiple genes that belong to the category of immediate early genes (IEGs) that are up-regulated.
source: As for the transNK3 cluster, we found multiple genes that belong to the category of immediate early genes (IEGs) were up-regulated (Nr4a1, Nr4a2, Nr4a3, Dusp1, Junb, Nfkbia, Nfkbid, Nfkbiz, Egr1, Supplementary file 1).
evidence: This is based on differential gene expression analysis with specific genes listed.

claim: TransNK3 cluster is transcriptionally similar to the novel NK_3 cluster defined previously in the mouse spleen.
source: This cluster is transcriptionally similar to the novel NK_3 cluster defined previously in the mouse spleen with up-regulation of genes including Pim1, Gadd45b, Bhlhe40, Irf8, Ccl3, Ccl4 besides the IEGs (Supplementary file 1; Crinier et al., 2018).
evidence: This is based on comparison with published data from Crinier et al., 2018.

claim: The Euclidean distance indicates transcriptional similarity between transNK1 and transNK2, both of which have higher transcriptional similarity to the iNK cluster than to termNK cluster.
source: The Euclidean distance indicated transcriptional similarity between transNK1 and transNK2, both of which had higher transcriptional similarity to the iNK cluster (Figure 2A).
evidence: This is shown in Figure 2A through hierarchical clustering analysis.

claim: TransNK3 has higher transcriptional similarity to the termNK cluster than to the iNK cluster.
source: In comparison, the transNK3 had higher transcriptional similarity to the termNK cluster (Figure 2A).
evidence: This is shown in Figure 2A through hierarchical clustering analysis.

claim: When NK clusters are ordered as iNK→transNK1→transNK2→transNK3→termNK, the module score based on up-regulated DEGs of iNK cluster gradually declines.
source: When we ordered the five clusters as iNK→transNK1→transNK2→transNK3→termNK, the module score based on the up-regulated DEGs of the iNK cluster or the down-regulated DEGs of the termNK cluster gradually declined (Figure 2B).
evidence: This is demonstrated in Figure 2B showing module score progression.

claim: When NK clusters are ordered as iNK→transNK1→transNK2→transNK3→termNK, the module score based on up-regulated DEGs of termNK cluster gradually increases.
source: In contrast, the module score based on the up-regulated DEGs of the termNK or the down-regulated DEGs of the iNK cluster gradually increased (Figure 2B).
evidence: This is demonstrated in Figure 2B showing module score progression.

claim: The pseudotime analysis indicates the maturation order of NK clusters with iNK and transNK1 at the beginning and termNK at the end of the trajectory.
source: Based on the transcriptional information, each cell from the five clusters were assigned to the pseudotime trajectory (Figure 2D). The pseudotime progression indicated the maturation order. As shown in Figure 2E, we picked the far-left side of the trajectory as the root point as we found cells from iNK and transNK1 clusters mostly resided here (Figure 2F). Based on this root point, the pseudotime dictated that the far-right side of the trajectory was the most mature population which was dominated by the termNK cluster (Figure 2E and F).
evidence: This is shown in Figure 2D, 2E, and 2F through Monocle2 pseudotime analysis.

claim: Nearly all Raptor-deficient CD3−CD122+ cells cluster distinctly from WT cells.
source: Strikingly, nearly all the Raptor-deficient CD3−CD122+ cells clustered distinctly from the WT cells (Figure 3A).
evidence: This is demonstrated in Figure 3A showing separate clustering.

claim: Cluster #8 in the Raptor analysis is ILC1 indicated by high expression of Tmem176a/b and Cxcr6.
source: The high expression of Tmem176a/b and Cxcr6 revealed Cluster #8 were ILC1 while all the rest seven clusters were NK cells (Figure 3—figure supplement 1B).
evidence: This is shown in Figure 3—figure supplement 1B with marker expression.

claim: mTORC1 is potentially dispensable for the development of ILC1.
source: As the expression of iCre driven by Ncr1 presumably also occurred in the ILC1, this data indicated that mTORC1 is potentially dispensable for the development of ILC1.
evidence: This is inferred from the observation that ILC1 cluster contains both WT and Raptor-deficient cells.

claim: All three Rictor-deficient NK cell-dominated clusters have high expression of up-regulated genes in the iNK cluster to the level similar to the least mature Cluster #1 of WT NK cells.
source: Interestingly, all three Rictor-deficient NK cells-dominated clusters (#5, 6, 7) had high expression of up-regulated genes in the iNK cluster to the level similar to the least mature Cluster #1 of WT NK cells (Figure 3E, iNK_up).
evidence: This is demonstrated in Figure 3E showing module score analysis.

claim: Nearly all Rictor-deficient NK cell-dominated clusters have more transcriptome similarity to the most immature cluster #1 and the less mature transitional cluster #2 of WT mouse.
source: Strikingly, the hierarchical clustering analysis indicated that nearly all the Rictor-deficient NK cell-dominated clusters (#5, 6, 7) had more transcriptome similarity to the most immature cluster #1 and the less mature transitional cluster #2 of WT mouse (Figure 3F).
evidence: This is shown in Figure 3F through hierarchical clustering analysis.

claim: The deep learning (DL) classifier is the most accurate machine-learning classifier with the lowest error rate for NK cell classification.
source: As summarized in the Figure 4—figure supplement 1A, the overall accuracy of all classifiers ranged from 60% to 70% with deep learning (DL) classifier being the most accurate with the lowest error rate.
evidence: This is shown in Figure 4—figure supplement 1A comparing classifier performance.

claim: All five NK clusters were identified by the classifiers except for the RF classifier which failed to detect the transNK3 subset.
source: Importantly, all five NK clusters were identified by the classifiers except for the RF classifier which failed to detect the transNK3 subset (Figure 4A).
evidence: This is demonstrated in Figure 4A showing classification results from different algorithms.

claim: The most dominant cluster of Raptor-deficient NK cells is transNK2 accounting for more than 50% of total Raptor-deficient NK cells.
source: The most dominant cluster of the Rptorfl/fl Ncr1Cre/WT mouse was transNK2 accounting for more than 50% of the total Raptor-deficient NK cells (Figure 4C).
evidence: This is shown in Figure 4C with machine-learning classification results.

claim: 50% of Rictor-deficient NK cells fall into the category of iNK cluster based on machine-learning classification.
source: The classification of Rictor-deficient NK cells resulted in 50% of all cells fell into the category of iNK cluster (Figure 4D and E and Figure 4—figure supplement 1C).
evidence: This is demonstrated in Figure 4E showing classification results.

claim: The classification of Rictor-deficient NK cells contradicts cell surface markers-defined maturity which revealed only terminal maturation defects.
source: This is a drastic contradiction to the cell surface markers-defined maturity which revealed only terminal maturation defects of Rictor-deficient NK cells (Figure 1—figure supplement 1B).
evidence: This is based on comparison between machine-learning classification results and flow cytometry data.

claim: There is almost no ILC1 and Cd3high cluster cells in the Tbx21−/− sample.
source: Illustrated by the distribution, there was almost no ILC1 (#8) and Cd3high (#9) cluster cells in the Tbx21−/− sample (Figure 5—figure supplement 1B).
evidence: This is shown in Figure 5—figure supplement 1B with cluster composition.

claim: T-bet is the master transcription factor of ILC1 lineage.
source: This was consistent with T-bet being the master transcription factor of ILC1 lineage (Klose et al., 2014), and the Cd3high cluster being a lineage related to NK-T cells which is nearly absent in Tbx21−/− mice (Townsend et al., 2004).
evidence: This is supported by citations to Klose et al., 2014 and Townsend et al., 2004.

claim: NK-T cells are nearly absent in Tbx21−/− mice.
source: This was consistent with T-bet being the master transcription factor of ILC1 lineage (Klose et al., 2014), and the Cd3high cluster being a lineage related to NK-T cells which is nearly absent in Tbx21−/− mice (Townsend et al., 2004).
evidence: This is supported by citation to Townsend et al., 2004.

claim: All three T-bet-deficient NK cell-dominated clusters present similar module score pattern as the immature cluster #1 in all up- or down-regulated DEGs of iNK or termNK cluster.
source: All three T-bet-deficient NK cells-dominated clusters (#5, 6, 7) presented similar module score pattern as the immature cluster #1 in all up- or down-regulated DEGs of iNK or termNK cluster (Figure 5A).
evidence: This is demonstrated in Figure 5A showing module score analysis.

claim: The transcriptional similarity between the least immature WT NK cells (Cluster #1) and the bulk T-bet-deficient NK cells (Clusters #5, #6, #7) is manifested by hierarchical clustering analysis.
source: The transcriptional similarity between the least immature WT NK cells (Cluster #1) and the bulk T-bet-deficient NK cells (Clusters #5, #6, #7) were further manifested by the hierarchical clustering analysis (Figure 5B).
evidence: This is shown in Figure 5B through hierarchical clustering.

claim: More than 60% of T-bet-deficient NK cells are categorized into the iNK cluster by machine-learning classifiers.
source: When we applied the machine-learning-based classifiers, more than 60% of the T-bet-deficient NK cells were categorized into the iNK cluster and there were only few cells in the transNK3 and termNK clusters (Figure 5C and D and Figure 5—figure supplement 1E).
evidence: This is demonstrated in Figure 5D showing classification results.

claim: T-bet deficiency results in up-regulation of immature NK signature genes and down-regulation of terminally mature NK genes.
source: Direct comparison of the bulk WT and Tbx21−/− NK cells in the scRNA-seq dataset revealed that T-bet deficiency resulted in up-regulation of immature NK signature genes and down-regulation of terminally mature NK genes (Figure 5E).
evidence: This is shown in Figure 5E with specific genes listed and their expression changes.

claim: Within 14 up-regulated genes in the iNK cluster, 10 genes have significantly increased expression in T-bet-deficient NK cells compared to WT NK cells.
source: Within the 14 up-regulated genes (average logFC ≥0.25) in the iNK cluster from three WT combined analysis, we found 10 of those genes with significantly increased expression in T-bet-deficient NK cells compared to WT NK cells (Figure 5E).
evidence: This is shown in Figure 5E listing specific genes.

claim: Within 56 termNK cluster signature genes, 18 genes have decreased expression in T-bet-deficient NK cells compared to WT NK cells.
source: Within the 56 termNK cluster signature genes (average logFC ≥0.25), we also observed decreased expression of 18 genes in T-bet-deficient NK cells compared to WT NK cells (Figure 5E).
evidence: This is shown in Figure 5E listing specific genes.

claim: 796 genes represent the transcriptional signature of the relatively immature CD27 SP NK subset.
source: In total, we found 796 genes representing the transcriptional signature of the relatively immature CD27 SP NK subset.
evidence: This is based on analysis of bulk RNA-seq dataset comparing CD27 SP with DP and CD11b SP NK cells.

claim: 796 immature NK signature genes are significantly enriched in T-bet-deficient NK cells compared to WT counterparts.
source: GSEA revealed that these 796 immature NK signature genes were significantly enriched in the T-bet-deficient NK cells comparing to the WT counterparts, emphasizing that T-bet is required to suppress the expression of genes associated with immature NK cells to a large extent (Figure 5G).
evidence: This is shown in Figure 5G through GSEA analysis.

claim: T-bet is required to suppress the expression of genes associated with immature NK cells to a large extent.
source: GSEA revealed that these 796 immature NK signature genes were significantly enriched in the T-bet-deficient NK cells comparing to the WT counterparts, emphasizing that T-bet is required to suppress the expression of genes associated with immature NK cells to a large extent (Figure 5G).
evidence: This is based on GSEA results shown in Figure 5G and represents an inference from the data.

claim: 654 T-bet-binding genes were identified from T-bet ChIP-seq dataset using splenic NK cells.
source: we reanalyzed the recently published T-bet ChIP-seq dataset generated using splenic NK cells and assessed whether T-bet directly targets the immature NK genes (Shih et al., 2016). With q-value set at 1 × 10−5 and focus on the protein-coding genes, we found a list of 654 T-bet-binding genes.
evidence: This is based on reanalysis of published ChIP-seq data from Shih et al., 2016.

claim: T-bet-binding genes are significantly depleted in the iNK cluster compared to all other cells.
source: We found a significant depletion of T-bet-binding genes in the iNK cluster compared to all other cells, indicating that T-bet does not directly bind to the majority of these iNK signature genes (Figure 6A, left).
evidence: This is shown in Figure 6A through GSEA analysis.

claim: T-bet does not directly bind to the majority of iNK signature genes.
source: We found a significant depletion of T-bet-binding genes in the iNK cluster compared to all other cells, indicating that T-bet does not directly bind to the majority of these iNK signature genes (Figure 6A, left).
evidence: This is inferred from the depletion of T-bet ChIP-seq peaks in iNK signature genes.

claim: T-bet-binding genes are significantly enriched in the termNK cluster compared to all other cells.
source: On the contrary, we found the T-bet-binding genes were significantly enriched in the termNK cluster comparing to all other cells (Figure 6A, right).
evidence: This is shown in Figure 6A through GSEA analysis.

claim: T-bet ChIP-seq peaks are significantly enriched in CD11b SP NK cells compared to CD27 SP compartment.
source: Similarly, when comparing the CD27 SP with the CD11b SP NK subset in the bulk RNA-seq dataset, we found significant enrichment of the T-bet ChIP-seq peaks in the CD11b SP NK cells compared to the CD27 SP compartment (Figure 6B).
evidence: This is shown in Figure 6B through GSEA analysis.

claim: Several immature NK signature genes that are up-regulated in T-bet-deficient NK cells have direct T-bet binding of regulatory regions.
source: Nevertheless, we found several immature NK signature genes that are up-regulated in T-bet-deficient NK cells with direct T-bet binding of the regulatory regions (Figure 6C).
evidence: This is shown in Figure 6C with examples of ChIP-seq peaks at specific gene loci.

claim: T-bet is unlikely to directly bind and suppress the bulk of the immature NK genes.
source: In conclusion, T-bet is unlikely to directly bind and suppress the bulk of the immature NK genes.
evidence: This is inferred from the depletion of T-bet ChIP-seq peaks in iNK signature genes.

claim: Transcription factor FoxO1 is enriched in T-bet-deficient NK cells compared to WT controls.
source: Interestingly, we found that transcription factor FoxO1 was enriched in the T-bet-deficient NK cells comparing to WT controls (Figure 6D), a phenomenon that we have previously established in the Rictor-deficient NK cells (Yang et al., 2018).
evidence: This is shown in Figure 6D through GSEA analysis and supported by previous work (Yang et al., 2018).

claim: The transcript level of Foxo1 is significantly higher in T-bet-deficient NK cells.
source: We also found the transcripts level of Foxo1 was significantly higher in the T-bet-deficient NK cells indicating that T-bet may suppress the expression of Foxo1 (Figure 6E).
evidence: This is shown in Figure 6E with TPM values from bulk RNA-seq.

claim: T-bet may suppress the expression of Foxo1.
source: We also found the transcripts level of Foxo1 was significantly higher in the T-bet-deficient NK cells indicating that T-bet may suppress the expression of Foxo1 (Figure 6E).
evidence: This is inferred from increased Foxo1 expression in T-bet-deficient cells.

claim: T-bet directly binds to the intron region and regulatory region upstream of transcription starting site of Foxo1 locus.
source: The direct binding of T-bet in the intron region and the regulatory region up-stream of transcription starting site of Foxo1 locus further supported this possibility (Figure 6F).
evidence: This is shown in Figure 6F with ChIP-seq peaks at Foxo1 locus.

claim: FoxO1 has the highest expression in the CD27 SP subset.
source: These data prompted us to hypothesize that Foxo1, which has the highest expression in the CD27 SP subset (Deng et al., 2015), is essential in driving the expression of immature NK signature genes.
evidence: This is supported by citation to Deng et al., 2015.

claim: FoxO1 is essential in driving the expression of immature NK signature genes.
source: These data prompted us to hypothesize that Foxo1, which has the highest expression in the CD27 SP subset (Deng et al., 2015), is essential in driving the expression of immature NK signature genes.
evidence: This is a hypothesis based on the enrichment of FoxO1 in immature NK cells and its increased activity in T-bet and Rictor-deficient cells.

claim: Hyperactive FoxO1 suppresses the expression of T-bet in Rictor-deficient NK cells leading to terminal maturation defects.
source: Previously we proposed that hyperactive FoxO1 suppresses the expression of T-bet in Rictor-deficient NK cells leading to the terminal maturation defects (Yang et al., 2018).
evidence: This is based on previous work by the authors (Yang et al., 2018).

claim: Deletion of Foxo1 in Rictor-deficient NK cells rescues the number of NK cells in the spleen to the level compatible to WT control.
source: Importantly, deletion of Foxo1 in Rictor cKO mice rescued the number of NK cells in the spleen to the level compatible to the WT control (Figure 7—figure supplement 1A and B).
evidence: This is shown in Figure 7—figure supplement 1A and B with quantification of NK cell numbers.

claim: Deletion of Foxo1 in Rictor-deficient NK cells completely rescues the percentage of CD11b SP subset and KLRG1+ NK cells to the level compatible to WT control.
source: Notably, deletion of Foxo1 in Rictor-deficient NK cells completely rescued the percentage of CD11b SP subset or the KLRG1+ NK cells to the level compatible to the WT control (Figure 7A and B, Figure 7—figure supplement 1C and D).
evidence: This is shown in Figure 7A and B with quantification of maturation markers.

claim: FoxO1 is the transcription factor suppressing the terminal maturation program in Rictor-deficient NK cells.
source: These data indicated that FoxO1 is the transcription factor suppressing the terminal maturation program in Rictor-deficient NK cells.
evidence: This is inferred from the rescue of maturation defects upon Foxo1 deletion.

claim: Deletion of Foxo1 in Rictor-deficient NK cells rescues the expression of T-bet in CD27 SP and DP subsets to the level of corresponding WT control.
source: Gated on three subsets of NK cells from the spleen, we found deletion of Foxo1 in the Rictor-deficient NK cells rescued the expression of T-bet in the CD27 SP and DP subsets to the level of the corresponding WT control (Figure 7—figure supplement 1E).
evidence: This is shown in Figure 7—figure supplement 1E with T-bet protein levels.

claim: The rescue of T-bet expression is incomplete in terminal CD11b SP NK compartments upon Foxo1 deletion in Rictor-deficient NK cells.
source: The rescue was incomplete in the terminal CD11b SP NK compartments (Figure 7—figure supplement 1E).
evidence: This is shown in Figure 7—figure supplement 1E with T-bet protein levels.

claim: Deletion of Foxo1 alone results in almost a fold increase of T-bet protein level in all three developmental stages compared to WT control.
source: Deletion of Foxo1 alone resulted in almost a fold increasing of the T-bet protein level in all three developmental stages compared to the WT control.
evidence: This is based on data from Figure 7—figure supplement 1E comparing Foxo1 single knockout to WT.

claim: In addition to FoxO1, other factors downstream of mTORC2 are involved in the regulation of T-bet expression.
source: These data indicated that, in addition to FoxO1, other factors downstream of mTORC2 are involved in the regulation of T-bet expression.
evidence: This is inferred from the incomplete rescue of T-bet expression in some NK subsets.

claim: Rictor/Foxo1 double knockout mouse harbors reduced percentage of iNK cluster and substantially increased percentage of termNK population compared to Rictor single knockout.
source: Compared to the Rictor cKO mouse, the Rictor/Foxo1 cDKO mouse harbored reduced percentage of iNK cluster and substantially increased percentage of termNK population indicating successful rescue of the Rictor-deficient NK cells via deletion of Foxo1 (Figure 7C).
evidence: This is shown in Figure 7C with machine-learning classification results.

claim: Rictor/Foxo1 double knockout mouse has reduced expression of iNK signature genes compared to Rictor single knockout.
source: We further explored the expression of the immature NK genes in both samples and found reduced expression of iNK signature genes in the Rictor/Foxo1 cDKO mouse compared to the Rictor cKO mouse (Figure 7D).
evidence: This is shown in Figure 7D with module score analysis.

claim: Rictor/Foxo1 double knockout mouse has increased expression of termNK signature genes compared to Rictor single knockout.
source: Consistent with the rescue, we also found increased expression of termNK signature genes in the Rictor/Foxo1 cDKO mouse compared to the Rictor cKO mouse (Figure 7D).
evidence: This is shown in Figure 7D with module score analysis.

claim: Both Rictor and FoxO1 are haplo-sufficient to the development of NK cells.
source: To ensure efficient generation of experimental mice with littermate control, we used Rictorfl/+Foxo1fl/+Ncr1Cre/WT mice as the WT control mice since both Rictor and FoxO1 are haplo-sufficient to the development of NK cells (data not shown).
evidence: This is stated by the authors based on their unpublished observations.

claim: There is a negative feedback loop between FoxO1 and T-bet that is part of what transcriptionally defines mature NK cells as a lineage.
source: We proposed that, in addition to the well-established role of FoxO1 in suppressing the expression of T-bet (Deng et al., 2015), T-bet can also suppress the expression of FoxO1 as the expression and activity of FoxO1 are increased in T-bet-deficient NK cells, and that this negative feedback loop is part of what transcriptionally defines mature NK cells as a lineage.
evidence: This is a hypothesis proposed by the authors based on their findings and previous literature.
